newsitem.title: THAILAND: Karen refugees head for long stay in Thai jungle.
newsitem.headline: Karen refugees head for long stay in Thai jungle.

text.p: Thousands of Karen refugees who fled Burmese soldiers face squalid living conditions and the threat of disease in the jungles of western Thailand, refugees and relief workers said on Saturday.

The refugees, mostly young children and elderly men and women, streamed into Thailand on oxcarts and trucks and by foot on Friday. They brought along belongings, cattle and pets -- signs that they expected to stay a while in Thailand.

"Villagers were evacuated from all 24 villages around Jaisong and Kwe Kler as Burmese soldiers advanced to our communities," Saw Po Tha Da, a refugee leader, told Reuters at his jungle camp at Perng Kerng.

"We do not know what to do next but we hope the Thai government can protect us from a Burmese onslaught," he said. He added that most new refugees were from Jaidong and Kwe Kler, Karen-dominated villages in Burma's Moulmein province, about seven km (four miles) from the Thai border.

The refugees, who deserted their homes after the camps of the Karen National Union (KNU) were overrun by Rangoon's troops this week, settled in scattered makeshift camps in Umphang district, border patrol police said.
The KNU, a predominantly Christian rebel group, has fought the Burmese military government for greater autonomy for the eastern Karen state since Burmese independence in 1948.
A KNU spokesman on Saturday denied speculation that the group's 71-year-old leader, General Bo Mya, was gravely ill.
Bo Mya's personal secretary, Ma Tha, told Reuters the rumours were groundless and said Bo Mya was fit and strong enough to lead the rebel group.
"Yesterday I was with the general. I don't believe he is suffering from sudden sickness," Ma Tha said.

About 4,000 refugees have set up temporary shelters at Perng Kerng, camping on the roadside, under trees and in bushes near small streams, from which they draw water for drinking, washing and feeding cattle.
"They risk getting diarrhoea and malaria living in such conditions," a Western doctor from a private relief organisation told Reuters.
He said at least 18 people had suffered from diarrhoea in the past three days and dozens, mostly children, were down with 'flu and colds.
"It is impossible to control outbreaks of diarrhoea and malaria," said the relief worker, who declined to be named.

Thailand had no estimate for how many new Karen refugees crossed the border since Burmese troops attacked the KNU mobile camps and headquarters with mortars and artillery and then overran them on Thursday and Friday.

"Nobody knows the precise number of new refugees because once they cross the border, they disappear into the jungles or take shelter with relatives in Thailand. I can only say there are over 10,000 of them," a border patrol police officer said.

"They began streaming in in big groups after (the) sound of heavy artillery fires in Burma in the past few days. We tried to stop them but they defied our orders," the policeman said at a border checkpoint.
He said the sound of gunfire remained audible late on Friday but the refugee influx had eased earlier on Friday.
More than 70,000 ethnic Karen refugees who fled earlier fighting inside Burma have lived in refugee camps near the Thai borders for years.
